variants.answer: I’d first define ingestion delay consistently—for example, the time from an event’s source timestamp to when it becomes queryable—and confirm the timestamps and clock synchronization are reliable. Then I’d instrument that end-to-end interval, segment it by source and pipeline stage, and capture a baseline across representative peak and off-peak periods. I’d report percentiles such as p50, p95, and p99, plus the share of events meeting the freshness target; an average alone can hide tail delays. I’d also record event volume, failures, and late or missing events so a lower delay isn’t mistaken for improvement when data is being dropped. After any change, I’d compare the same metrics over comparable traffic windows, check for regressions by source, and use a sustained trend or controlled rollout rather than a single favorable data point to decide whether we improved.”

variants.answer: I’d agree on what counts as ingestion delay, then measure it from the event’s creation time until it is available to users. I’d establish a baseline over a representative period and track p50 and p95 delay, broken down by source. I’d compare those numbers after changes under similar traffic and also watch error rates, to make sure faster ingestion isn’t coming at the cost of lost data.
